text: The 2007 World Series was the championship series of Major League Baseball's (MLB) 2007 season and the 103rd edition of the event. It was a best-of-seven playoff between the National League (NL) champion Colorado Rockies and the American League (AL) champion Boston Red Sox, with the Red Sox sweeping the Rockies in four games. This marked the Rockies' first and only World Series appearance as of 2025. Boston’s victory was their second World Series title in four seasons, their second consecutive sweep, and their seventh overall; it also represented the third sweep in four years by AL champions. The series began on Wednesday, October 24 and concluded on Sunday, October 28. Terry Francona became the second Red Sox manager to win two World Series titles, following Bill Carrigan, who won in 1915 and 1916. Including the last three games of the AL Championship Series, the Red Sox outscored their opponents 59–15 over their final seven games. Francona also became the first manager to win his first eight World Series games. The Rockies became the first NL team to be swept in a World Series after previously sweeping the League Championship Series, and only the second team ever to suffer such a fate, following the Oakland Athletics in 1990; this outcome would later be repeated by the 2012 Detroit Tigers, who were swept by the San Francisco Giants after sweeping the New York Yankees in the ALCS. As of the end of the 2024 season, 2007 remains the most recent season an American League team has swept a National League team in the World Series. This was the fourth time since interleague play began in 1997 that a World Series matchup was a rematch from the regular season, with the Rockies having defeated the Red Sox 2–1 in a three-game series at Fenway Park from June 12–14. Over 29 days in September through mid-October, the Rockies won 21 games and lost only once, including sweeps of the Philadelphia Phillies in the NLDS and the Arizona Diamondbacks in the NLCS, and a win over the San Diego Padres in the NL Wild Card tie-breaker. Their 2007 run was one of the most unlikely postseason runs in MLB history, having just 33/1 odds at the start of the season to win the National League. The Rockies' eight-day layoff was the longest in MLB postseason history, caused by their NLCS sweep, the ALCS going seven games, and scheduling by MLB. The Red Sox were more conventionally dominant, leading the American League East for most of the season. In the postseason, they swept the Los Angeles Angels of Anaheim in the ALDS and defeated the Cleveland Indians in the ALCS after trailing 3–1, winning the final three games by a combined score of 30–5. Several players from the famed 2004 curse-breaking Red Sox team remained with the team. Neither team had participated in the previous year's postseason. Under the 2006 Collective Bargaining Agreement, the Red Sox had home-field advantage in the World Series following the AL's 5–4 win in the 2007 All-Star Game, with the first two games in Boston and games 3 and 4 in Denver. On October 17, 2007, a week before the first game, the Rockies announced that tickets would be available only through online sales, despite prior plans for local retail outlets. Five days later, California-based ticket vendor Paciolan, Inc., the sole authorized distributor, suspended sales after less than an hour due to an excessive number of purchase attempts. The Rockies organization claimed it was a denial-of-service attack, prompting the FBI to begin its own investigation. Ticket sales resumed the next day, with all three home games selling out within 2+1⁄2 hours. The Red Sox relied primarily on online sales for tickets, though some Fenway Park tickets were sold by phone and at the box office. They held a random drawing for the right to buy postseason tickets on October 15, with winners purchasing at a private online sale. Street prices in Boston were lower than in 2004: according to StubHub, the average price was about $1500 in 2007, down $300 from three years prior. Some fans found it cheaper to travel to Denver than to pay street prices for Boston tickets. Boston won the series 4–0. In Game 1, the Red Sox won by a blowout behind ALCS MVP Josh Beckett, who struck out nine batters, including the first four he faced, over seven innings for his fourth postseason win. Mike Timlin and Éric Gagné pitched perfect eighth and ninth innings, respectively. Boston Hall of Famer Carl Yastrzemski threw the ceremonial first pitch, as he had in Game 1 of 2004. Rookie Dustin Pedroia led off the first inning with a home run over the Green Monster in Fenway Park off Jeff Francis; it was only the second lead-off home run to start a World Series (the other being Don Buford’s in 1969). Kevin Youkilis then doubled to right, moved to third on David Ortiz’s groundout, and scored on Manny Ramirez’s single. After Mike Lowell flew out, Jason Varitek singled before J. D. Drew doubled to score Ramirez and make it 3–0 Red Sox. The Rockies scored in the second when Garrett Atkins doubled with one out off Beckett and scored on Troy Tulowitzki’s double, one out later, but the Red Sox got the run back when Youkilis walked with two outs and scored on Ortiz’s double. In the fourth, the Red Sox loaded the bases with two outs on a single, double, and intentional walk, and Varitek’s two-run double put them up 6–1. They extended the lead with seven runs in the fifth: Julio Lugo hit a leadoff single off Franklin Morales, Jacoby Ellsbury bunted into a forceout at second, Pedroia popped out, a balk moved Ellsbury to second, and he scored on Youkilis’s double. Ortiz’s double and Ramirez’s single scored a run each. The Red Sox loaded the bases on a double and walk before Drew’s single scored another run. Ryan Speier relieved Morales and walked all three batters he faced to force in three more Boston runs. Matt Herges relieved Speier and got Youkilis to fly out to right to end the inning. Though Herges and two relievers held Boston scoreless for the rest of the game, the Red Sox finished with 13 runs, the most ever in a World Series Game 1, and tied another record with nine extra-base hits. The last 11 of the Red Sox runs came with two outs. The ceremonial first pitch in Game 2 was thrown by 13-year-old heart transplant recipient Andrew Madden, accompanied by Hall of Famer Dwight Evans. After the Game 1 debacle, the Rockies appeared to return to form, scoring quickly on a groundout by Todd Helton with runners on second and third in the first. However, this was the only time the Rockies led in the series. Postseason veteran Curt Schilling (5+1⁄3 IP, one run, four hits) and Boston’s bullpen (Okajima, 2+1⁄3 IP; Papelbon, 1+1⁄3 IP) allowed no other runs. The Red Sox tied the game in the fourth off Ubaldo Jimenez on Jason Varitek’s sacrifice fly with runners on second and third, then took the lead in the next inning on Mike Lowell’s RBI double with runners on first and second. Matt Holliday had four of Colorado’s five hits in Game 2, including a base hit off Papelbon with two outs in the eighth. Before throwing another pitch, Papelbon caught Holliday leaning too far off first base and picked him off—Papelbon’s first career pickoff. This was the first World Series game ever played in Colorado, lasting 4 hours and 19 minutes, making it the longest nine-inning game in World Series history. Game 3 was also the 600th World Series game ever played. Daisuke Matsuzaka pitched five innings of scoreless ball and left in the sixth with no runs allowed. The Red Sox scored six runs in the third inning: Jacoby Ellsbury hit a leadoff double, moved to third on Dustin Pedroia’s single, and scored on David Ortiz’s double. After Manny Ramirez was intentionally walked, Mike Lowell’s single scored two more runs. J. D. Drew popped out before Ramirez was thrown out at home on Jason Varitek’s single with Lowell advancing to third. After Julio Lugo walked to load the bases, Matsuzaka hit a two-run single for his first base hit and RBI in the Major Leagues. Ellsbury capped the scoring with his second double of the inning to knock Colorado starter Josh Fogg out of the game. The Rockies’ offense responded in the sixth and seventh innings against a shaky Boston bullpen. After Matsuzaka walked two straight in the sixth with one out, reliever Javier López allowed back-to-back RBI singles to Brad Hawpe and Yorvit Torrealba. Mike Timlin allowed two straight leadoff singles in the seventh before NLCS MVP Matt Holliday brought the Rockies within one with a three-run home run off Hideki Okajima. Brian Fuentes gave back those runs in the eighth by walking Lugo with one out and allowing a subsequent single to Coco Crisp before Ellsbury and Dustin Pedroia, who had four and three hits respectively, hit back-to-back RBI doubles, raising Boston’s lead to 9–5. Jonathan Papelbon came on for a four-out save, getting Holliday to fly out on one pitch, leaving runners on first and second. Jason Varitek added Boston’s tenth run in the top of the ninth off LaTroy Hawkins with a sacrifice fly, scoring Mike Lowell, who had just stolen third base—the first time a Red Sox baserunner stole third base in the World Series since 1975—after hitting a leadoff single and moving to second on a sacrifice bunt. Papelbon came back out in the bottom of the ninth to complete the save, getting the first two outs before surrendering a two-out triple to Brad Hawpe, then finishing with a groundout from Yorvit Torrealba. The Red Sox won Game 3 10–5. During Game 3, the Red Sox set several World Series records: they struck early with Ellsbury’s leadoff double and Pedroia’s groundout, followed by Ortiz’s RBI single. Series MVP Mike Lowell hit a leadoff double in the fifth and scored on Varitek’s single, making the score 2–0 Boston. In the seventh, Lowell hit a home run to give Boston a 3–0 lead and knock starter Aaron Cook out of the game. The Rockies responded when Brad Hawpe hit a home run off a Manny Delcarmen fastball, bringing them within two. Relief pitcher Brian Fuentes gave back that run when Boston pinch-hitter Bobby Kielty hit a ball into the left field stands on the first pitch of the inning, extending the Red Sox lead to 4–1. In the bottom of the inning, Hideki Okajima allowed a one-out single to Todd Helton followed by a Garrett Atkins two-run home run, bringing the Rockies within one. Jonathan Papelbon relieved Okajima and earned his third save of the series. At 12:06 a.m. EDT on Monday, October 29, Papelbon struck out Colorado pinch hitter Seth Smith for the final out of the 2007 season. Boston had won its second World Series title in four years and seventh all-time. There was controversy in the top of the eighth when Fox’s broadcast announced that Alex Rodriguez would be opting out of his contract with the Yankees to become a free agent. Commissioner Bud Selig stated that an embargo had been placed on all Major League Baseball stories until the top event ended. Rodriguez and his agent Scott Boras later apologized for the incident. The Rockies became the third team in Series history (the 1937 Yankees and 1966 Orioles being the others) not to commit an error in a World Series of any length, and they were the first team to do so while losing the World Series. 2007 World Series (4–0): Boston Red Sox (A.L.) beat Colorado Rockies (N.L.). While the celebratory crowd at Kenmore Square was not as unruly as in 2004, cars were overturned and 37 arrests were made. The Red Sox victory parade, again in duck boats and called a "Rolling Rally" as in 2004, took place on October 30, 2007, with closer Jonathan Papelbon performing his infamous "Irish Jig" while local punk band the Dropkick Murphys played their hit "I'm Shipping Up to Boston." The Red Sox World Series win in 2007 continued the success of Boston-area teams in recent years: the Celtics won their 17th championship, their first since 1986, the last time the Red Sox lost in the World Series, 7+1⁄2 months later; they would win their 18th championship in 2024. The New England Patriots had victories in 2001, 2003, 2004, 2014, 2016, and 2018, the Boston Bruins in 2011, and the Red Sox in 2004, 2013, and 2018. The World Series was televised by Fox in the United States, with Joe Buck and Tim McCarver as booth announcers, starting at 8:00 pm EDT (6:00 pm MDT). The series broke with the tradition of starting on a Saturday, as MLB had become convinced that weekend games drew lower television ratings; prior to this season, every World Series since 1985 had opened on a Saturday, except for 1990. This was the first World Series to start on a Wednesday since 1968. Rogers Sportsnet (RSN) in Canada used the MLB International feed with Dave O'Brien and Rick Sutcliffe as booth announcers. NASN showed the games live to most of Europe, while in the UK, all games were shown terrestrially on Five. NHK aired the series in Japan. On radio, the series was broadcast nationally by ESPN Radio with Jon Miller and Joe Morgan announcing. Locally, Joe Castiglione and Glenn Geffner called the series for the Red Sox on WRKO in Boston, while Jack Corrigan and Jeff Kingery called it for the Rockies on KOA in Denver. Per contractual obligation, non-flagship stations on the teams' radio networks carried the ESPN Radio broadcasts. The Red Sox won two more World Series titles in 2013 and 2018; both were managed by members of the 2007 team. Pitching coach John Farrell served as skipper of the 2013 Red Sox, featuring 2007 holdovers Clay Buchholz (DNP), Jacoby Ellsbury, Jon Lester, David Ortiz, and Dustin Pedroia. The 2018 Red Sox were managed by Alex Cora, an infielder on the 2007 team. The Red Sox finished as a wild-card team in 2008, winning 95 games, and were defeated in the ALCS by the Tampa Bay Rays in seven games. They again qualified as a 95-win wild-card team in 2009 but lost 3–0 to the Los Angeles Angels in the ALDS. In both 2010 and 2011, the Red Sox missed the postseason despite winning 89 and 90 games, respectively. The 2011 season saw the Red Sox hold a nine-game lead in the wild card heading into September, only to lose 13 of their final 20 games and miss the playoffs, leading to the dismissal of skipper Terry Francona and the end of an era. By their next championship in 2013, they had both a new general manager and manager. The Rockies’ World Series run was nicknamed “Rocktober,” a portmanteau of the Rockies team name and October.

The 2018 Red Sox were managed by Alex Cora, who had previously been an infielder on the 2007 Red Sox team. In 2008, the Red Sox finished as a wild-card team with a 95-win record and were defeated in the ALCS by the Tampa Bay Rays in seven games. They again secured a 95-win wild-card spot in 2009 but lost 3–0 to the Los Angeles Angels in the ALDS. In both 2010 and 2011, the Red Sox missed the postseason despite winning 89 and 90 games, respectively. The 2011 season saw the Red Sox hold a nine-game lead in the wild card heading into September, only to lose 13 of their final 20 games, resulting in missing the playoffs and leading to the dismissal of manager Terry Francona, marking the end of an era for Red Sox baseball. By their next championship in 2013, the team had appointed a new general manager and manager. The Rockies' World Series run was nicknamed “Rocktober,” a portmanteau of the team name and October. After reaching the World Series in 2007, the Rockies appeared in the playoffs only three times in the following 15 seasons, with 2007 being their sole World Series berth. In 2009, the Rockies earned a wild-card berth after winning 92 games, but lost in four games to the Philadelphia Phillies in a rematch of the 2007 NLDS. During that season, the Rockies fired Clint Hurdle and replaced him with Jim Tracy. Between 2010 and 2017, the Rockies never finished higher than third place in the NL West, though in 2017 they returned to postseason play as a second wild-card team, losing in the Wild Card Game to the Arizona Diamondbacks. The following season, the Rockies made consecutive postseason appearances for the first time in team history, winning the Wild Card Game against the Chicago Cubs but losing in the NLDS to the Milwaukee Brewers 3–0. After managing the Rockies, Hurdle was hired by the Pittsburgh Pirates in 2011 and in 2013 ended a 20-year major North American professional sports record without a winning season. Under Hurdle, the Pirates made the postseason three consecutive years, winning the 2013 National League Wild Card Game during that span. Three members of the 2007 Rockies went on to win a World Series ring with other teams: outfielder Matt Holliday won in 2011 with the St. Louis Cardinals, pitcher Jeremy Affeldt won in 2010, 2012, and 2014 with the San Francisco Giants, and pitcher Franklin Morales won in 2013 with the Red Sox and in 2015 with the Kansas City Royals.
